title: Northern Hemisphere
description: Half of Earth that is north of the Equator
wiki_lead:
The Northern Hemisphere is the half of Earth that is north of the equator. For other planets in the Solar System, north is defined as being in the same celestial hemisphere relative to the invariable plane of the Solar System as Earth's North Pole.
Due to Earth's axial tilt of 23.439281°, there is a seasonal variation in the lengths of the day and night. There is also a seasonal variation in temperatures, which lags the variation in day and night. Conventionally, winter in the Northern Hemisphere is taken as the period from the December solstice (typically December 21 UTC) to the March equinox (typically March 20 UTC), while summer is taken as the period from the June solstice through to the September equinox (typically on 23 September UTC). The dates vary each year due to the difference between the calendar year and the astronomical year. Within the Northern Hemisphere, oceanic currents can change the weather patterns that affect many factors within the north coast. Such events include El Niño–Southern Oscillation.
Trade winds blow from east to west just above the equator. The winds pull surface water with them, creating currents, which flow westward due to the Coriolis effect. The currents then bend to the right, heading north. At about 30 degrees north latitude, a different set of winds, the westerlies, push the currents back to the east, producing a closed clockwise loop.
Its surface is 60.7% water, compared with 80.9% water in the case of the Southern Hemisphere, and it contains 67.3% of Earth's land. The continents of North America and mainland Eurasia are located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere, together with about two-thirds of Africa and a small part of South America.

Geography and climate
During the 2.5 million years of the Pleistocene, numerous cold phases, called glacials (Quaternary ice age), or significant advances of continental ice sheets, in Europe and North America, occurred at intervals of approximately 40,000 to 100,000 years. The long glacial periods were separated by more temperate and shorter interglacials which lasted about 10,000–15,000 years. The last cold episode of the last glacial period ended about 10,000 years ago. Earth is currently in an interglacial period of the Quaternary, called the Holocene. The glaciations that occurred during the glacial period covered many areas of the Northern Hemisphere.

The Arctic is a region around the North Pole (90° latitude). Its climate is characterized by cold winters and cool summers. Precipitation mostly comes in the form of snow. Areas inside the Arctic Circle (66°34′ latitude) experience some days in summer when the Sun never sets, and some days during the winter when it never rises. The duration of these phases varies from one day for locations right on the Arctic Circle to several months near the Pole, which is the middle of the Northern Hemisphere. grok_lead: The Northern Hemisphere is the half of Earth north of the Equator, an imaginary line encircling the planet at 0Â° latitude that divides it into northern and southern portions. Astronomically, it is defined as the region north of the celestial equator. This hemisphere covers approximately 50% of Earth's total surface area, but its composition differs markedly from the Southern Hemisphere, with about 40% land and 60% ocean coverage compared to the southern portion's 20% land and 80% ocean. It contains roughly 68% of the planet's total landmass, hosting the entirety of the continents of North America, Europe, and Asia, as well as the northern portions of South America and Africa. The Arctic Ocean lies entirely within the Northern Hemisphere, while the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans span both hemispheres, with the majority of the Pacific and Indian Oceans in the Southern Hemisphere, influencing global weather patterns and marine ecosystems. The Northern Hemisphere is home to approximately 90% of the world's human population (as of 2026), concentrated in urban centers across Asia, Europe, and North America due to the availability of arable land and historical settlement patterns. Its geography drives significant climatic diversity, from the frozen Arctic tundra to tropical rainforests near the Equator, but the disproportionate land coverage leads to greater seasonal temperature swings than in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere, as land heats and cools more rapidly than water. Seasons hereâsummer, autumn, winter, and springâresult from Earth's 23.5Â° axial tilt, with the North Pole leaning toward the Sun during June to August (summer) and away during December to February (winter), opposite to the Southern Hemisphere 's cycle. This tilt also affects phenomena like the midnight sun in polar regions during summer and polar night in winter, while mid-latitudes experience moderate variations in daylight and temperature. Ecologically and meteorologically, the Northern Hemisphere plays a pivotal role in global systems, including the circulation of major ocean currents like the Gulf Stream, which moderates climates in western Europe, and atmospheric patterns such as the jet stream that influence weather across continents. It encompasses diverse biomes, supporting biodiversity hotspots and agricultural heartlands that feed billions. Recent climate data indicate accelerated warming in this hemisphere, with 2024 remaining the warmest year on record for Northern Hemisphere surface temperatures as of 2026.
